steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our CLoVe paper, about making contrastive vision-language models like CLIP better at compositional language without losing their performance on standard object recognition benchmarks. Cover the motivation, the trade-off in existing methods, and our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Progress of vision-language models and their wide use
2. The weakness: compositionality
3. Why compositionality matters; no model solves it yet
4. Prior fixes and their cost on object-centric recognition
5. Our framework and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. VLM progress
- big increase in Vision and Language task performance, last few years
- VLMs like CLIP: used in many settings, directly or as foundational models; remarkable performance across tasks

2. Compositionality weakness
- excel at object-centric recognition, but text representations seem invariant to word order
- fail to compose known concepts in novel ways
- Figure 1: CLIP top on ImageNet, behind on compositionality benchmarks

3. Why it matters
- needed to recognize more complex concepts in images; text-to-image models generating novel scene with specific constraints
- example: image of "the woman shouts at the man" -> who shouts at whom
- no evidence any VLM identifies compositions, incl. large single-stream models like GPT-4V
- compositionality benchmarks still an open challenge

4. Prior fixes
- NegCLIP, REPLACE: increase compositional capabilities of pre-trained VLMs
- cost: lower object-centric recognition (ImageNet, EuroSAT, CIFAR100)
- NegCLIP: SugarCrepe 72.9% -> 82.5%, ImageNet top-1 63.4% -> 55.8%
- REPLACE: SugarCrepe 84.7%, ImageNet down to 52.9%

5. Ours
- framework: improve existing two-tower models on compositional language, keep standard benchmark performance (Figure 1)
- data curation matters for compositional knowledge
- hard negatives -> additional improvements
- model patching preserves performance on previous tasks
- combined = CLoVe; improves compositionality over contrastively pre-trained VLM
- case study: CLIP
- upon publication: checkpoints to substitute CLIP-like weights

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Vision and Language tasks have seen a big increase in performance in the last few years. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like CLIP have been used in many settings, either directly or indirectly as foundational models, and they showed remarkable performance on several tasks.

These models are very good at object-centric recognition, but the text representations they learn seem to be invariant to word order, and they fail to compose known concepts in novel ways. For example, as Figure 1 shows, CLIP has top performance on ImageNet tasks but it falls behind on compositionality benchmarks.

Language compositionality is essential for recognizing more complex concepts in images, or for making text-to-image models successfully generate a novel scene with specific constraints. For example, in an image showing “the woman shouts at the man,” you need to recognize who is shouting at whom to understand the scene correctly.

4. Prior fixes
- NegCLIP, REPLACE increase compositional capabilities of pre-trained VLMs
- cost: object-centric recognition drops (ImageNet, EuroSAT, CIFAR100)
- NegCLIP: SugarCrepe 72.9% -> 82.5%, ImageNet top-1 63.4% -> 55.8%
- REPLACE: SugarCrepe 84.7%, ImageNet 52.9%

5. Ours
- improve two-tower models on compositional language, keep standard benchmarks (Figure 1)
- contributions: data curation; hard negatives; model patching; combined into CLoVe
- case study CLIP; checkpoints upon publication

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Vision and Language tasks have seen a big increase in performance in the last few years. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like CLIP have been used in many settings, either directly or indirectly as foundational models, and they showed remarkable performance on several tasks.

These models are very good at object-centric recognition, but the text representations they learn seem to be invariant to word order, and they fail to compose known concepts in novel ways. For example, as Figure 1 shows, CLIP has top performance on ImageNet tasks but it falls behind on compositionality benchmarks.

Language compositionality is essential for recognizing more complex concepts in images, or for making text-to-image models successfully generate a novel scene with specific constraints. For example, in an image showing “the woman shouts at the man,” you need to recognize who is shouting at whom to understand the scene correctly.

But there is no evidence that any VLM, including large-scale single-stream models like GPT-4V, identifies compositions successfully. This is supported by the fact that existing benchmarks that test compositionality are still an open challenge.

To address these limitations, previous work introduced techniques to increase the compositional capabilities of pre-trained VLMs, like NegCLIP and REPLACE. But these methods have a significant cost: they sacrifice performance on more common object-centric recognition, as measured by ImageNet, EuroSAT, and CIFAR100. For example, as Figure 1 shows, NegCLIP increased (compared to the pre-trained model) its ability on the SugarCrepe compositionality benchmark from 72.9% to 82.5%, but at the same time its ImageNet top-1 accuracy dropped from 63.4% to 55.8%. In the same way, prior work applied REPLACE and reached a high score of 84.7% on SugarCrepe, but its ImageNet accuracy dropped significantly to 52.9%.

In this paper we introduce a framework that significantly improves the ability of existing two-tower models to encode compositional language while keeping their performance on more standard benchmarks, as Figure 1 shows. Our contributions are the following. First, we show that data curation can have a significant impact on how a model handles compositional knowledge. Second, we confirm that training with hard negatives can bring additional improvements. Third, we show experimentally that model patching can be used to preserve model performance on previous tasks. Finally, we combine these ideas into a new framework called CLoVe and show that it can significantly improve compositionality over a contrastively pre-trained VLM. As a case study, we show how our framework can effectively improve CLIP’s compositional abilities while keeping the performance on other tasks. Upon publication we will provide checkpoints that others can use to replace their CLIP-like model weights with a version that has significantly better language composition abilities.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
There has been a significant increase in the performance of Vision and Language tasks over the last few years [1,2,3,4,5]. Vision-Language Models (VLMs), such as CLIP [1], have been leveraged in multiple settings, either directly or indirectly as foundational models, and have demonstrated remarkable performance across several tasks [6,7,8,3,9,10].

Such models excel at object-centric recognition, yet they learn text representations that seem invariant to word order [11,12,13] and fail to compose known concepts in novel ways [14,15]. For example, as shown in Figure 1, CLIP has top performance on ImageNet tasks but falls behind on compositionality benchmarks.

Language compositionality is essential for recognizing more complex concepts in images or for making text-to-image models successfully generate a novel scene with specific constraints [16]. For instance, in an image depicting “the woman shouts at the man,” it is essential to recognize who is shouting at whom in order to understand the scene correctly.

Yet there is no evidence that any VLM, including large-scale single-stream models such as GPT-4V [17], identifies compositions successfully. This is supported by the fact that existing benchmarks testing compositionality remain an open challenge [11,12,14,15].

To address these limitations, previous work has introduced techniques to increase the compositional capabilities of pre-trained VLMs, such as NegCLIP [12] and REPLACE [15]. However, these methods come at a significant cost: they sacrifice performance on more common object-centric recognition, as measured by ImageNet [18], EuroSAT [19,20], and CIFAR100 [21]. For instance, as shown in Figure 1, NegCLIP increased (compared to the pre-trained model) its ability to address the SugarCrepe [15] compositionality benchmark from 72.9% to 82.5%, while its ImageNet [18] top-1 accuracy dropped from 63.4% to 55.8%. Similarly, [15] applied REPLACE to reach a high score of 84.7% on SugarCrepe, but at the cost of a significant drop in ImageNet accuracy to 52.9%.

In this paper, we introduce a framework that significantly improves the ability of existing two-tower models to encode compositional language while keeping their performance on more standard benchmarks, as shown in Figure 1. Specifically, our contributions are as follows. First, we show that data curation can significantly affect how a model handles compositional knowledge. Second, we confirm that training with hard negatives can bring additional improvements. Third, we show experimentally that model patching can be employed to preserve model performance on previous tasks. Finally, we combine these ideas into a new framework called CLoVe and show that it can significantly improve compositionality over a contrastively pre-trained VLM. As a case study, we show how our framework can effectively improve CLIP’s compositional abilities while maintaining performance on other tasks. Upon publication, we will provide checkpoints that others can use to replace their CLIP-like model weights with a version that has significantly better language composition abilities.
